vignette:
Amir, a forty-year-old software engineer, presented as a man holding himself together with immense, exhausting effort. It had been seven months since the earthquake that had torn through the city where he was attending a conference. The physical injuries had healed, but he spoke of the time since as a slow collapse. The event itself remained a chaotic blur in his mind, a collection of searingly vivid but untethered moments. He remembered the violent lurch of the hotel conference room, the horrifying grinding sound of the building twisting, and the sudden, choking darkness filled with dust and screams. He could not, however, string these fragments into a coherent timeline. Sometimes, sitting in the quiet of his home office, he would hear that grinding noise again, so clearly that he would grip his desk, convinced the walls were about to give way. The memory that felt most real, the one that would sometimes hijack all his senses at once, was of the stampede for the emergency exit. In that chaos, a man had shoved him aside with such force that Amir fell, his head striking the floor. The memory came with the sharp pain, the feeling of powerlessness, and the sight of the man's desperate face disappearing into the crowd.

In the aftermath, lying on a cot in a makeshift triage center, the sounds of sirens and suffering had seemed to burn into his brain. This experience cemented a profound aversion that now dictated parts of his life. He recently cancelled his annual physical, telling his wife, Layla, that he was too busy with a project deadline. The thought of a clinical setting, even the sight of an ambulance on the street, sent a jolt of panic through him that he couldn't explain or control. This was one of many new rules in his life. At his open-plan office, he could no longer tolerate his assigned desk in the middle of the floor. He insisted on a corner spot, his back to two walls, where no one could approach him unseen. A colleague walking briskly past his periphery was enough to make him flinch violently, his body reacting as if to an imminent attack. He had come to believe that constant vigilance was the only thing keeping him safe. Before entering any room-a meeting room, a coffee shop, a movie theater-he would first have to locate every exit, mapping a mental blueprint for escape before he could even begin to relax.

This constant threat-monitoring was draining, leaving little room for anything else. He felt a profound sense of alienation from the man he used to be. He remembered being easygoing, quick to laugh. Now, he felt he was "always miserable." He looked at his life and saw only the potential for future loss, a conviction that "nothing good can happen to me anymore." This belief was tangled with a persistent, bitter self-reproach. He would replay the moment he was pushed, convinced that someone else, a better or stronger man, would not have let it happen. He felt he should have anticipated the danger, that his fall was a personal failing. This thought often led him down a darker path. At night, when sleep wouldn't come, he would lie awake and ruminate for hours about finding the man who pushed him, imagining scenarios of confrontation and revenge. These thoughts offered a fleeting sense of power but left him more agitated and exhausted.

To combat the rising tide of fear and misery, Amir adopted a strategy of forced positivity. Whenever a memory fragment or a dark thought surfaced, he would internally chant, "I am safe, everything is fine, think of something good," a desperate attempt to pave over the turmoil. But the tension remained. The most painful consequence of his transformation had been in his marriage. A few weeks ago, Layla had come up behind him while he was washing dishes and gently placed a hand on his back. He had cried out and spun around, his arms raised defensively. The hurt in her eyes was worse than any anger. That was the night she told him she felt she was living with a stranger, that she missed being able to touch her own husband. It was this moment of stark, relational loss that finally propelled him to seek help, terrified that the happy man he once was had not just been lost in the earthquake, but was gone for good.
